introduction-the-connection-storm.core: Every new database connection costs a TCP handshake, maybe TLS, authentication and megabytes of memory. When thousands arrive at once (a connection storm), the database spends all its CPU saying hello and none running queries.

first_principles.problem: During a flash sale, 10,000 app threads open connections at the same moment. Each request is individually valid, but together they make the database spend 100% of its CPU on handshakes and authentication, and queries stop.
truths: Opening a connection is real work: TCP, TLS, auth, memory.
Traffic spikes make many clients connect at once.
Aggregate behaviour only shows up under load.
derivation: Count the cost per connection: **3-way TCP handshake**, **TLS** round trips, **auth** lookups, **2–10 MB RAM** (Postgres).
Multiply by thousands during a spike: CPU goes to setup, not SQL.
Stop clients from talking to the database directly. Put a **proxy** in between that keeps a few long-lived connections.

analogy.title: A chef who greets every guest
analogy.story: On a Friday night, every guest insists the head chef personally greets and seats them. With 10 guests that's charming. With 10,000 arriving together, the chef never cooks a meal.
analogy.breaks: Guests leave eventually. Application connections often stay open and idle, still holding memory on the database.

example.title: Autoscaling makes it worse
example.scenario: Load rises, the app autoscales from 50 to 400 pods, each opening 25 connections.

steps.label: Cascade
steps.detail: Slower queries trigger more autoscaling, which opens even more connections.

steps.label: Fix
steps.detail: Pods connect to a proxy, and the proxy keeps 100 warm connections to the DB.

example.outcome: you can recognise a connection storm and why scaling the app can deepen it.

points: Insert a proxy to absorb them.

check.q: Why does a connection storm happen even with correct application code?
check.a: Each connection is valid. The failure comes from thousands of them at once overwhelming the database's setup work.

what-is-a-database-proxy.core: A database proxy speaks the database's wire protocol, so unlike a TCP load balancer it understands each SQL statement and can pool, route, cache or block it.

first_principles.problem: A generic load balancer just forwards bytes. It can't tell a SELECT from an UPDATE, can't cache a result, and can't refuse a dangerous query. To manage database traffic intelligently, something must understand it.
truths: Decisions about queries need to see the queries.
derivation: Sit between apps and database, speaking the **wire protocol** (Layer 7).
Parse each statement and decide: **pool, route, cache, block**.
Pick by ecosystem: **ProxySQL** (MySQL routing, cache, firewall), **PgBouncer** (lightweight PG pooling), **RDS Proxy** (managed, IAM, failover), **Pgpool-II**, **Vitess** (sharding).

analogy.title: A mail sorter vs. a mail truck
analogy.story: A truck (load balancer) carries sealed bags without knowing what's inside. A sorter (proxy) opens envelopes, reads addresses, sends urgent ones by courier, answers some from a template, and bins junk mail.
analogy.breaks: Mail sorters add little delay. A proxy adds a network hop and becomes critical infrastructure that must be highly available itself.

example.title: Same traffic, two layers

steps.label: L4
steps.detail: The NLB has no idea it's a SELECT and sends it to whatever backend is next.

steps.label: L7
steps.detail: ProxySQL recognises a read, checks its cache, then picks a healthy replica.

example.outcome: you can explain why protocol awareness enables every advanced proxy feature.

points: That enables pooling, routing, caching, firewalling.

check.q: Proxy vs load balancer in one sentence?
check.a: A load balancer forwards TCP streams blindly (L4). A database proxy parses the SQL protocol (L7) and can act on each query.

connection-multiplexing-the-core-feature.core: Multiplexing maps many cheap client connections onto a few long-lived database connections (M:N), lending a backend connection only while a query or transaction runs. The database sees a stable, small number regardless of traffic.

first_principles.problem: Without a proxy, every app thread needs its own database connection (1:1). The database's connection count, and its memory and CPU overhead, rises and falls with application concurrency.
truths: Accepting a TCP connection is cheap for a lightweight proxy.
Database connections are expensive but reusable.
Most client connections are idle at any instant.
derivation: **Frontend**: the app opens as many connections to the proxy as it likes (e.g. 10,000).
**Backend**: the proxy keeps a **fixed, pre-authenticated pool** (e.g. 50).
**Borrow and return**: per query or transaction, lend an idle backend and return it in microseconds.
Pick a mode: **session** (safest), **transaction** (best default), **statement** (rare).
Beware session state (`SET search_path`, advisory locks) under transaction pooling.

analogy.title: Shared bikes
analogy.story: A city doesn't give every resident a bike. A dock holds 50 bikes, and anyone takes one for a trip and docks it again. Thousands of people are served by 50 bikes because rides are short.
analogy.breaks: Riders leave nothing on the bike. Database sessions can carry settings, and the next borrower inherits or loses them depending on pooling mode.

example.title: 10,000 app connections on 50 backends
example.scenario: A Node.js fleet with PgBouncer in transaction mode.

steps.label: Elastic app
steps.detail: The app can scale to any number of pods without touching DB limits.

steps.label: Caveat
steps.detail: Any `SET` must be inside the transaction (`SET LOCAL`).

example.outcome: database load is decoupled from application concurrency.

points: Transaction pooling is the usual choice.

check.q: Why does session pooling barely help?
check.a: Each client holds a backend for its whole session, even when idle, so backend count still tracks client count.

query-caching-offloading-reads-transpare.core: A proxy like ProxySQL can cache result sets for queries matching a rule, with a TTL, so repeated reads never reach the database and no application changes are needed. There's no active invalidation, so use it only for data that can be slightly stale.

first_principles.problem: Application caches (Redis) need code for cache checks, invalidation and TTLs. MySQL's built-in query cache was removed in 8.0 because its global mutex serialised writes. Teams still want to offload repetitive reads without touching code.
truths: Many queries are repeated with identical text and parameters.
A proxy sees every query and can answer before the database does.
Without invalidation, cached data ages until its TTL.
derivation: Define **rules** (regex on query text) with a **cache_ttl** (e.g. 60 s).
First match goes to the DB and the result is stored, keyed by **normalised query + parameters**.
Later matches within the TTL are answered from proxy memory.
Accept: **in-memory only**, **no active invalidation**, so use it for catalogues and config, not balances or inventory.

analogy.title: A receptionist with a cheat sheet
analogy.story: Visitors keep asking the same questions ("what are your opening hours?"). The receptionist writes the answer on a cheat sheet and repeats it for the next hour without phoning the manager. If the hours change, visitors get the old answer until the sheet is rewritten.
analogy.breaks: A receptionist might hear that the hours changed. The proxy never does. It will serve stale results until expiry.

example.title: Offloading product lookups
example.scenario: Product detail queries are 40% of DB reads and change rarely.

steps.label: Load
steps.detail: `LOAD MYSQL QUERY RULES TO RUNTIME`, live with no restart.

steps.label: Scope
steps.detail: Never cache stock or price-at-checkout queries.

example.outcome: a large slice of read load disappears from the database with zero application changes.

check.q: Why is a proxy cache wrong for account balances?
check.a: Without invalidation, a changed balance could be served stale for the whole TTL, which is unacceptable for transactional data.

readwrite-splitting-routing-by-query-int.core: A proxy can send writes to the primary and SELECTs to replicas by inspecting each statement, putting idle replicas to work without app changes. Reads that must see a just-made write need an exception rule to the primary.

first_principles.problem: You have replicas, but the app connects to one endpoint, so the replicas sit idle. Rewriting a legacy app to keep separate read and write pools and route every query is slow and error-prone.
truths: The first keyword of a statement reveals intent (SELECT vs INSERT…).
Some reads must see the latest write.
derivation: Register **hostgroups**: writer (primary) and readers (replicas).
**Route by keyword**: INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/DDL go to the writer, SELECT to the readers (round-robin or weighted).
Send **locking reads** (`SELECT … FOR UPDATE`) to the writer.
Add **high-priority exceptions** for read-after-write queries, and remove lagging replicas (`max_replication_lag`).

analogy.title: A post office with two counters
analogy.story: Sending a parcel (write) goes to the main counter. Checking a parcel's status (read) goes to self-service kiosks. But if you just posted something, the kiosks may not have updated yet, so for that you go back to the main counter.
analogy.breaks: People know when they just posted something. The proxy doesn't, so read-after-write cases must be identified and given explicit rules.

example.title: "My order isn't showing"
example.scenario: After checkout, the confirmation page SELECTs the new order and it's sometimes missing.

steps.label: Diagnose
steps.detail: The confirmation read landed on a lagging replica.

steps.label: Fix
steps.detail: Add a higher-priority rule matching the confirmation query digest that routes to the writer hostgroup.

steps.label: Guard
steps.detail: Replicas lagging more than 2 s are pulled from the pool automatically.

code.text:
INSERT INTO mysql_query_rules (rule_id, active, match_digest, destination_hostgroup, apply)
VALUES (1, 1, '^SELECT .* FROM orders WHERE id = \? /\* fresh \*/', 10, 1),
       (2, 1, '^SELECT.*FOR UPDATE', 10, 1),
       (3, 1, '^SELECT', 20, 1);

example.outcome: replicas carry most reads, and users still see their own new data.

check.q: Which reads are unsafe to send to replicas?
check.a: Reads that must reflect a just-committed write (read-your-own-writes) and locking reads like SELECT … FOR UPDATE.

query-firewall-and-observability.core: Because a proxy sees every statement, it can block dangerous query patterns before they reach the database, and its per-digest statistics show the most expensive queries across 100% of traffic without enabling the slow log.

first_principles.problem: A bad query (an unbounded scan, a likely injection, a runaway report) reaches the database before anyone can stop it. And finding the top offenders usually means enabling slow-query logs on the database itself, which add overhead and only catch queries above a threshold.
truths: Patterns of dangerous SQL are recognisable.
Blocking before execution costs nothing on the database.
Aggregating by normalised query shape reveals where time goes.
derivation: Add **firewall rules**: match a pattern and return an `error_msg` instead of routing.
Block **unbounded scans**, suspicious **unparameterised** queries, and enforce **rate limits** or **kill long runners**.
Read **stats_mysql_query_digest**: per normalised query, call count, total and min/max time.
Read **stats_mysql_connection_pool**: backend health, used/free, latency per hostgroup.

analogy.title: A security gate with a turnstile counter
analogy.story: The gate refuses anyone carrying something dangerous before they enter the building, and the turnstile counts every visitor and how long they stayed, so you know who uses the building most without following anyone around inside.
analogy.breaks: A gate checks obvious items. Pattern rules can be bypassed by unusual SQL, so a firewall complements, not replaces, parameterised queries and DB permissions.

example.title: Finding and blocking a costly query
example.scenario: MySQL CPU is high, and the slow log is off.

steps.label: Find
steps.detail: The top digest by `sum_time` is `SELECT * FROM users` with no WHERE, from an admin export.

steps.label: Block
steps.detail: A rule returns "full scans of users are not allowed".

steps.label: Follow up
steps.detail: The admin tool gets fixed to paginate.

example.outcome: the costliest query is found without touching the database configuration and stopped at the door.

points: Block dangerous SQL at the proxy.
No slow-log overhead on the DB.

check.q: How do you find the top 5 expensive queries without the slow log?
check.a: Query the proxy's stats_mysql_query_digest, ordered by total execution time.
